segments.text: Hey everyone, Peter Zion here, coming to you from central Yosemite, just south of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Quartzite Peak. This is a very difficult place to get to. In my opinion, the view

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: makes it worth it, but it's two days of off-trail travel in the most rugged parts

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: of the park. Let's talk about something else that we hope is worth it, and that is

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: green tech, solar and wind particularly. Now, photovoltaic cells are... they're

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: heralded as a cure-all. The idea is you can put them anywhere, get a little bit of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: juice from the Sun, it's better than any sort of fossil fuels, and that is total

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: and absolute crap. The process for producing PVs is extraordinarily damaging

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: to the environment if it's done wrong, and even if it's done right, it's a bit of a

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: question as to whether or not you can put the panels in the right place. Now, the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: silicon that goes into the PV panels themselves is not hard to get. Silicon is

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: one of the more common elements, and you can mine quartz in a lot of places. Then

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: there are half a dozen places that can refine it into solar-grade silicon. However,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: that process basically involves a blast furnace, and if you're doing this in

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: China, which is where nearly half of it is done, you're talking about doing it with

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: coal. So already the carbon footprint for the process is extreme. And then most of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: the assembly for the panels is done in China as well, usually in places like

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Zhejiang where it's done by slave labor. So already you've got all these things

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: that are kind of stacking up against solar right from the get-go. Now this is all

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: okay, right? If you're able to get an environmental benefit on the back end. Well,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: there are a lot of places in the world that are not particularly sunny, and most of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: those are places where we have our big cities. So for example, here I am in the highlands of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: the Sierras. If I was to put panels here, they'd do really well. We're at high elevation. They have

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: a lot of long sun days. It would be fine. Unfortunately, not a lot of people live here.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Take those same panels, and you move them to Seattle or Toronto or New York or Boston or London or

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Copenhagen or Stockholm or Shanghai or Hong Kong, and they're gonna generate less than

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: one-fifth the amount of electricity. So whatever you're willing to suck up on the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: front end, you need those panels to run five times as long in order to make good.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: And in most of those cities that I listed, that means you will never break even on

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: just the carbon debt to say nothing of the trade issues or the human rights issues.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Now, does that mean that solar is pointless and you can't put it anywhere? Of course not.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: If you're going to put it in a sunny place, say Albuquerque, New Mexico, where I live in

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Denver, Durban, South Africa, most places in, say, Italy or Greece, there are a lot of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: places where it makes a lot of sense. But there are far more where it makes none

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: whatsoever. And then, of course, there's a transmission issue. You don't put panels in

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: New York because it's too densely populated. You have to put them outside of the city, and if you

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: want to put them outside the city far enough away that they actually generate a

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: meaningful trickle of power, you're talking then about wiring at at least 500

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: miles. And now you have another issue with transmission and all the things that go

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: with that. So that's solar. Wind. Much better. There's nothing toxic involved in the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: manufacturing. A lot of the manufacturing is either done in the United States or in

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Denmark. You're using some sort of carbon fiber and then some aluminum. There is a

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: carbon footprint to both of those, but it's nothing compared to what you have to do

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: for silicon. And unlike solar, which seems to have this mystique, wind doesn't. No one

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: thinks that they should put wind turbines where it's not windy, but people think

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: that they should put solar panels where it's not sunny. And so wind turbines are

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: only going up in places that it makes sense. So American Great Plains are great, for

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: example. There's some places in California that are good. In the case of Europe,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: anywhere in the vicinity of the North Sea looks great. The Danes get about half of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: their power from wind. And then there are a number of places around the world that

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: look good as well. There's still the problem of co-locating that production with

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: population centers, but it's not nearly as messy in the case of wind because we're

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: now seeing a technological advance with wind. It used to be that the turbines were

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: only 100 feet tall. And so unless you had wind right there on the ground, it didn't

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: make much sense. But as our engineering has improved, it's gone to 200, 300, 40, now

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: almost 800 feet. And that means there's larger parts of the planet. We've seen like a

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: quadrupling of zones of the planet where wind now makes sense. And as you reach

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: higher, something else happens. You tap wind currents that are not just stronger, that

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: are more reliable. I'm going to rotate a little bit here so you can see more of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the view. That's where I went like four years ago. Anyway, because of that, for per

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: dollar invested in wind versus solar, you're going to generate about three to

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: four times as much electricity. In addition, those stronger, more reliable

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: currents can now start to be used for baseload capacity, which is really

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: important. One of the problems we have with wind versus solar and wind versus

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: solar versus everything else is intermittency. Obviously, the wind doesn't

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: always blow, and there has never been one iota of solar energy generated after

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: sunset. And yet, prime demand in most cities in the world is after 6 p.m. for

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: electricity. And that means solar can never be part of peak demand, but now wind

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: can. So, not only you're getting that three or four to one price difference in

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: terms of solar versus wind, wind is actually more useful overall because the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: wind can burn, or sorry, the wind can blow at times when we need the power the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: most. Now, the problem we have is that everyone has believing this mystique on

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: solar, and so in most populated zones in most of the planet, solar has become part of

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the environmental problem rather than part of the solution. And until we can get

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: past that, until we can actually match technologies to locations, the green

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: movement is actually, in many cases, causing more damage than help. Except for

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: wind. Wind is great. Okay, that's it for me. Until next time.
